title: AAP Just Swept Punjab's Municipal Elections. The Numbers Are Not Even Close.
excerpt: Bhagwant Mann's party won over 880 wards across 8 municipal corporations, 75 councils, and 20 nagar panchayats. Congress came a distant second. BJP finished behind independents.
body:
The Aam Aadmi Party has delivered a comprehensive victory in Punjab's urban local body elections, winning more than 880 wards across the state and establishing dominance in virtually every tier of municipal government. The results, which came after voting on May 26, confirm that AAP's hold on Punjab extends well beyond the state legislature.

Across 8 municipal corporations, 75 municipal councils, and 20 nagar panchayats, the party led by Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann swept the field. In the municipal council category alone, AAP won 759 of the 1,577 declared wards — nearly half the total. Congress came a distant second with 303 seats, followed by the Shiromani Akali Dal at 179 and the BJP at just 103.

## Municipal Corporations: AAP Dominant

In the eight municipal corporation races — which include Punjab's largest cities — AAP secured commanding majorities. The party's performance was particularly strong in Amritsar (41 of 52 wards), Sangrur (55 of 74), and Ludhiana (56 of 112). Even in Bathinda, traditionally a stronghold of the Akali Dal, AAP took 57 wards to SAD's 65, a significant improvement from previous cycles.

In Patiala, AAP won 41 of 92 wards. In S.A.S. Nagar (Mohali), the party secured 57 of 118 wards, outpacing Congress at 17 and BJP at 24.

## The Surprise: Independents Outperform BJP

Perhaps the most striking result was not a party victory at all. Independent candidates collectively won 226 wards — more than double the BJP's 103. In several smaller municipal bodies, independents emerged as the dominant force. In Bareta, independents claimed 11 of 13 wards, leaving AAP with just two. In Joga and Boha nagar panchayats, independents won majority seats.

The BJP, which had hoped to make inroads in Punjab ahead of the next assembly elections, finished fourth overall — behind AAP, Congress, and independents. The result is a setback for the party's expansion strategy in a state where it has historically struggled to gain traction.

## Why It Matters for the Diaspora

Punjab has one of the highest rates of emigration in India. An estimated 2.5 to 3 million Punjabis live abroad, with large concentrations in Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, and Australia. Municipal governance directly affects the cities and towns that NRI Punjabis call home — from infrastructure and road conditions to property development and public sanitation.

AAP's sweep could accelerate its infrastructure push in Punjab's cities. The party has made urban development — including road construction, sewer systems, and water supply — a centrepiece of its governance agenda. For NRIs with property in Punjab, the continuity of AAP governance at both the state and municipal level means a more predictable policy environment.

## Congress Holds Pockets, SAD Fades

Congress managed to hold ground in select areas, notably Kapurthala, where the party won 31 of 50 wards under the influence of the Rana family. In Firozpur, Congress edged AAP with 28 wards to 26. But these were exceptions. In most districts, Congress was a clear second.

The Shiromani Akali Dal, once the dominant force in Sikh-majority Punjab, continued its decline. The party's 179 wards represented just 11 percent of the total, its worst showing in municipal elections in decades.

## The Road Ahead

Over 7,500 candidates contested the elections, many of them independents who entered after being denied party nominations. The high independent tally suggests internal party dissent remains a factor, but it did not meaningfully dent AAP's overall performance.

With state assembly elections still some time away, the municipal results give Bhagwant Mann a strong mandate to continue shaping Punjab's urban landscape. For the opposition, the message is stark: AAP's grip on Punjab is, for now, firm and deepening.
author: Diaspora Desk
